sections.heading: C — Alcohol and Other Drugs
sections.markdown:
## C — Alcohol and Other Drugs

FACT_ID: sec11-F01 | anchor: A01
Alcohol is a factor in more than eighteen thousand fatal motor vehicle crashes every year in the United States, about forty percent of the total, and that is every driver's problem whether or not the driver drinks [A01].
Why it matters: the national figure is printed on the page and is a likely statistic question.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-F02 | anchor: A01
The drinking-driver problem reaches far beyond alcoholics; anyone who drives after taking alcohol, even the alcohol in a medicine, is part of it, because alcohol and other drugs cloud judgment and make people misjudge their own intoxication [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-F03 | anchor: A01
A large share of the solution rests with you as a driver: understand what alcohol and other drugs do to you, know your limits and stay within them, and do not drive after taking an intoxicant [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-F04 | anchor: A01
Alcohol is a depressant, not a stimulant; it slows reflexes, interferes with judgment, reduces alertness and impairs vision, and any feeling of stimulation comes only from lowered inhibitions that cost you caution and self-control [A01].
Why it matters: the depressant-not-stimulant distinction is a classic test item.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-F05 | anchor: A01
It makes no difference whether you drink beer, wine, whiskey or another beverage, because the amount of alcohol that reaches your blood is what causes the problem [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-F06 | anchor: A01
Alcohol can affect you differently at different times, and a small amount on an empty stomach acts more rapidly than it would after a recent meal [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-F07 | anchor: A01
Once alcohol is in your blood nothing can lessen its effect; black coffee, food or a cold shower may wake you up but will not sober you up, because only time lets the liver burn the alcohol and the kidneys and lungs eliminate it [A01].
Why it matters: only time sobers you; coffee and showers are the standard wrong answers.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-F08 | anchor: A01
Hawaii prohibits operating a motor vehicle while under the influence of intoxicants [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-F09 | anchor: A01
Under implied consent, anyone who operates a motor vehicle on Hawaii's public highways is deemed to have consented to a test of the amount of alcohol in the blood [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-F10 | anchor: A01
Under administrative license revocation your license is taken away and you receive a thirty-day temporary driving permit if a test shows a blood alcohol content of point zero eight or more or if you refuse the test, and anyone whose license is revoked may request a hearing [A01].
Why it matters: revocation follows either a failed test or a refusal, and the temporary permit lasts thirty days.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec11-F11 | anchor: A02
Under the zero tolerance rule a driver under twenty-one may not operate a motor vehicle with a blood alcohol content of point zero two or more [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec11-F12 | anchor: A02
A police officer who believes a driver is under the influence may request a test, and refusing can bring license revocation for one year, two years or four years depending on the driver's prior alcohol enforcement contacts [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec11-F13 | anchor: A02
A driver who refuses the test may still be charged with driving under the influence, and the test can also prove that a driver is not under the influence [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec11-F14 | anchor: A02
When a test shows alcohol in the blood, a driver is considered impaired at a blood alcohol content above point zero five percent but below point zero eight percent, and under the influence at point zero eight percent or more [A02].
Why it matters: point zero five to point zero eight is impaired; point zero eight and up is under the influence.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec11-F15 | anchor: A02
Consuming or possessing an alcoholic beverage anywhere on a public highway or a public sidewalk is illegal [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec11-F16 | anchor: A02
Keeping an opened alcoholic beverage container in the part of a motor vehicle normally occupied by the driver or passengers is prohibited on any public road [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec11-F17 | anchor: A02
Many drugs interfere with safe driving, including some in medicines your doctor prescribes and some in medicines sold without a prescription, so ask your doctor about any driving-related effects before taking a medicine [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec11-F18 | anchor: A02
Some over-the-counter allergy remedies and cold pills contain ingredients that can affect your driving ability [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec11-F19 | anchor: A02
Amphetamines, found in stimulants and diet pills and known on the illegal market as pep pills and speed, and overdoses of tranquilizers or sedatives known as downers, greatly impair driving and can by themselves cause death [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec11-F20 | anchor: A02
Combining alcohol with drugs can produce a far stronger effect than either one alone, so never mix alcohol and drugs [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec11-F21 | anchor: A02
Some of the most dangerous drugs, such as LSD, heroin and cocaine, can be obtained only illegally, they can make users completely unaware of or indifferent to their surroundings, and anyone under their influence must not try to drive [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec11-F22 | anchor: A02
Every drug on the illegal market is dangerous because there is no way to be certain of its strength or purity [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0056]

Misconceptions: alcohol is a depressant even though it can feel stimulating; coffee, food and cold showers wake you but never sober you, only time does; the kind of drink does not matter, only the amount of alcohol in the blood; refusing the breath or blood test still brings revocation and can still lead to a driving under the influence charge; the under-twenty-one limit is point zero two, far below the adult point zero eight; impaired begins above point zero five while under the influence begins at point zero eight.

Mnemonics: Point zero two for under twenty-one, above point zero five is impaired, point zero eight is under the influence; refusal means thirty days of temporary permit then one, two or four years of revocation; only time sobers you.

Glossary: depressant (a substance that slows the nervous system, as alcohol does); implied consent (the agreement to be tested that every driver gives by driving on public roads); administrative license revocation (loss of the license through the licensing agency after a failed or refused test, with a right to a hearing); zero tolerance (the near-zero alcohol limit for drivers under twenty-one); open container (an opened alcoholic beverage kept in the passenger area).

Dynamic facts: the national fatal-crash statistic is a figure that changes year to year and is stated only as this edition prints it; the thresholds, revocation periods and permit length are statutory values stable within this printing.

corpus_stability.reason: The Hawaii Driver's Manual is a periodically reprinted reference (imprint HMG 5/2023, copyright line through 2023); the the scale of the drinking-driver problem, how alcohol acts on the body, the implied consent and administrative revocation laws, zero tolerance for drivers under twenty-one, impairment thresholds, open container rules and the effects of prescription, over-the-counter and illegal drugs rules on pages 55–56 are statutory and procedural content that changes less than once a year, so no BlockedProbe.
